facts.claim: The Attorney-General's Department's Notice of Intended Marriage publication page (last updated 22 December 2022) says section 42 of the Marriage Act 1961 requires that a marriage shall not be solemnised unless a notice in writing of the intended marriage (this form) is given to the authorised celebrant solemnising the marriage. The form is downloadable as PDF and DOCX.

AGD: from 12 June 2024 the Notice of Intended Marriage may be witnessed remotely; the Marriage Act was amended to permanently give couples the option of having the NOIM witnessed in person or remotely by a facility that enables audio and visual communication between people in different places.

AGD: the requirements for authorised witnesses remain unchanged and location-dependent. If the couple is in Australia, the person remotely witnessing the NOIM (which can include an authorised celebrant) must also be in Australia. If the couple is outside Australia, the authorised witness (which cannot be a celebrant) must also be outside Australia. A NOIM for a person or couple outside Australia cannot be witnessed online.
AGD: authorised witnesses are listed in the 'Signatures of parties and witnesses' section of the Notice of Intended Marriage form.

The Attorney-General's Department's list of prescribed authorities says a prescribed authority is an officer or employee of the Commonwealth, a State or Territory appointed by the Attorney-General, and is authorised, among other things, to authorise a marriage celebrant to proceed with a marriage ceremony where the minimum one-month notice has not been provided (shortening of time). The list is searchable by state and territory and includes registrars and deputy registrars of local courts and state registries of births, deaths and marriages.

insider_details.detail: For an Australian ceremony the NOIM window is at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the date, so couples planning a long engagement should lodge once the date and celebrant are locked, not before the 18-month mark.

Couples living overseas can still complete the NOIM before flying home to marry in Australia, and since 12 June 2024 it can be witnessed by audio-visual link as well as in person, but the celebrant must still meet each partner separately and in person before the wedding, so build that meeting into the arrival schedule.

A NOIM is only needed for a marriage solemnised in Australia. A destination wedding abroad cannot be performed by an Australian celebrant or registered here; the paperwork instead runs through the destination's own requirements, often a CNI, which DFAT can issue but some countries only accept if issued locally.

Couples who legally marry abroad cannot then lodge a NOIM and marry again in Australia if the overseas marriage is recognised; a home celebration becomes a vow renewal or recommitment ceremony instead.
For a Greek Orthodox wedding in Australia the priest is also the civil celebrant, so the NOIM is signed with the priest; the Archdiocese asks for at least one calendar month and preferably three.

Order documents early: the celebrant needs evidence of date and place of birth, identity and proof any earlier marriage has ended. Divorce or death certificates for a previous spouse are the slowest to locate, especially from overseas registries.
